policy_title: Build 1.5 Million New Homes and Reform Planning
stated: Labour aims to build 1.5 million new homes over the next parliament by updating the National Policy Planning Framework, restoring mandatory housing targets, and strengthening the presumption in favour of sustainable development. They will fund additional planning officers by increasing the stamp duty surcharge for non-UK residents, prioritize brownfield development, and take a strategic approach to greenbelt ('grey belt') land release for new towns and urban extensions. Compulsory purchase compensation rules will be reformed to ensure fair compensation and speed up site delivery.

source.quote: Labour will get Britain building again, creating jobs across England, with 1.5 million new homes over the next parliament. We will immediately update the National Policy Planning Framework to undo damaging Conservative changes, including restoring mandatory housing targets. We will take tough action to ensure that planning authorities have up-to-date Local Plans and reform and strengthen the presumption in favour of sustainable development. Labour will support local authorities by funding additional planning officers, through increasing the rate of the stamp duty surcharge paid by non-UK residents. Labour will take a brownfield first approach, prioritising the development of previously used land wherever possible, and fast-tracking approval of urban brownfield sites. Without changing its purpose or general extent, Labour will take a more strategic approach to greenbelt land designation and release to build more homes in the right places. The release of lower quality ‘grey belt’ land will be prioritised and we will introduce ‘golden rules’ to ensure development benefits communities and nature. In partnership with local leaders and communities, a Labour government will build a new generation of new towns, inspired by the proud legacy of the 1945 Labour government. Alongside urban extensions and regeneration projects, these will form part of a series of large-scale new communities across England. We will introduce effective new mechanisms for cross-boundary strategic planning. Labour will reform compulsory purchase compensation rules to improve land assembly, speed up site delivery, and deliver housing, infrastructure, amenity, and transport benefits in the public interest. We will take steps to ensure that for specific types of development schemes, landowners are awarded fair compensation rather than inflated prices based on the prospect of planning permission.

bearing_set.reason: Directly targets housing supply (1.5m homes), affordability via tenure mix, and planning reform — core indicators of affordable housing access.

Strategic grey belt land release and large-scale construction create a concrete mechanism: new development on semi-natural land increases surface runoff (water quality indicator) and construction activity affects local air quality; brownfield priority offers a partial positive offset, making the net effect genuinely mixed and non-negligible.

Compulsory purchase compensation reform explicitly makes it easier for the state to acquire land at below-market rates, directly bearing on property rights — a named O10 indicator — through a concrete coercive mechanism (state appropriation of private land with altered compensation terms).

UK housing undersupply is a well-documented drag on labour mobility and productivity; a credible 1.5-million-home programme would affect workers' ability to locate near jobs, business investment decisions, and aggregate real living standards — a concrete O13 mechanism distinct from the distributional O1 and O4 channels.

Housing supply is the primary driver of the wealth gap between existing homeowners and renters/younger non-owners; moderating house-price growth narrows the Gini on wealth and the intergenerational fairness of asset gains — concrete mechanism to a specific O14 indicator.

membership_note: Five fundamentals warranted: the policy's core is O1 (housing supply/affordability); it has well-mechanised cross-outcome effects on O6 (land/nature at scale), O10 (CPO and property rights), O13 (productivity/labour mobility), and O14 (wealth inequality between owners and non-owners). No clear bearing on O2 (housing costs land in O1; essentials basket not directly affected), O11 (stamp-duty surcharge on non-UK residents is a narrow funding mechanism, not a material household tax-burden change), or O12 (no large unfunded spending implied; revenues roughly matched to planning officer costs).
